analysis.title: A Fat Cat in a Small Door
key_insights: The roughly $200bn UST Bond futures contract has become significantly negatively convex for the first time since early 2007, driven by a cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) shift risk in the delivery basket.

Bond futures conversion factors are set from a fixed matrix of coupon and maturity and ignore yield level. When the 20yr rate is above the 6% contract coupon, the longest-maturity bonds become CTD. Below 6%, the shortest become CTD.
From late 2008 until this summer the 20yr rate was well below 6%, so the CTD was almost certainly one of the shortest bonds in the basket and CTD shift risk was minimal.
With the December 2026 contract near 111.26 and the 20yr rate near 5% in early July, one bond had zero net basis and was the CTD. That CTD had a Duration of 11.03.

Once the futures price fell below 110, the Delivery Option, owned by futures shorts, became valuable. Longs no longer know their interest rate exposure, and the conversion table creates negative convexity for the contract.

The CTD moved to a bond with Duration 11.63 when the contract was near 106.78. With the 20yr rate near 5.68% (contract 102.25), the CTD is a 13.24 Duration bond, about 20% longer than a few weeks ago. Managers holding a fixed risk level would need to shed or hedge about 20% of their fixed-income risk.

The current CTD Duration of 13.24 would shorten to 11.03 on a 70bp rate decline and extend to 17.47 on a 70bp rate rise. The contract falls faster and rises slower near a CTD shift, and managers must buy as prices rise and sell as prices fall.

Bassman suggests the recent rapid rise in rates may be linked to CTD extension and hedge selling by risk managers. He cites the significant decline in CFTC-reported positioning as support. The effect is pro-cyclical: each hedge sale pushes rates higher and can trigger another CTD shift to a longer Duration bond.
A 20yr rate above 6% would extend the CTD to a Duration above 17. Bassman estimates this equals the Treasury auctioning about $110bn of 20yr bonds over four months.
Hedge fund basis traders may close out positions by selling Treasuries, adding sell pressure. The 20yr rate last breached 6% in November 1999.

Bassman calls the 10yr TIPS real rate of 2.90% the market 'waving the white flag' on a fiscal problem rather than a monetary or inflation problem. He cites a 6.2% fiscal deficit and lists fiscal reforms (lifting the $184,500 Social Security tax cap, raising the retirement age, means testing, ending step-up basis, reviving Simpson-Bowles, immigration reform).
Mortgage-backed securities trade 75bp to 100bp above 10yr Treasuries in yield because of negative convexity.
Bassman flags an upcoming ETF listing from Michael Green that monetizes the 'alpha factor' of passive investing, and says he may join.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Up from near 5% in early July. The level is approaching the 6% contract coupon, where the CTD would extend to the longest bonds and negative convexity hedging could accelerate selling.
Bassman reads this as the market signaling a fiscal credibility problem, not a monetary or inflation problem.
Cited as the basis for proposing a medium-term path to narrow the deficit.
Below the 110 level where the Delivery Option became valuable. The contract is now in the negatively convex zone.

risk_factors: A 20yr rate crossing 6.0% would extend the CTD Duration above 17, forcing more hedge selling, equivalent to about $110bn of 20yr issuance over four months.
Pro-cyclical negative convexity: hedge selling pushes rates higher, which triggers further CTD shifts to longer Duration bonds.
Basis trader unwinds at large hedge funds could add Treasury selling.
Fiscal credibility concerns, with a 6.2% deficit and a 2.90% 10yr real rate.
vol_and_positioning: CFTC-reported Treasury futures positioning has declined significantly, which Bassman cites as support for the view that risk managers hedged into the rate rise.
The UST Bond futures contract is negatively convex for the first time since early 2007, so hedgers buy as prices rise and sell as prices fall.
Bassman calls a 20yr rate of 6% 'a bubbling Convexity Vortex'.
Large hedge fund basis traders may close out positions by selling Treasuries, adding to selling pressure.

theme_stances.key_argument: The UST Bond futures contract has become negatively convex as the CTD shifts longer, so hedge selling may have contributed to the rate rise and could accelerate near 6%.
A 2.90% 10yr real rate signals a fiscal problem, not a monetary or inflation one.
theme_stances.evidence: we have a problem of "Trust", not inflation
